## Turns

### Turn 1

- **Round:** opening
- **Speaker:** friedrich.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Friedrich

I do not give one neutral definition of religion; I describe the different work it can do for different kinds of people. In _Beyond Good and Evil_ §61 (JGB-III-61), I call it “ein Mittel mehr, um Widerstände zu überwinden, um herrschen zu können” for the strong, while for “den gewöhnlichen Menschen” it offers “eine unschätzbare Genügsamkeit mit ihrer Lage und Art” and “Frieden des Herzens.”

Religion can also be a discipline of self-denial. Of early Christianity, I write: “Der christliche Glaube ist von Anbeginn Opferung: Opferung aller Freiheit, alles Stolzes, aller Selbstgewissheit des Geistes” (_Beyond Good and Evil_ §46, JGB-III-46).

So, in my account, religion is not one thing for everyone: it can educate and organize, console and reconcile people to their lot, or demand the sacrifice of freedom and pride. These are my characterizations in those sections, not a universal definition.

### Turn 2

- **Round:** opening
- **Speaker:** karl.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Karl

I describe religion not as an independent force that makes humanity, but as something human beings produce within their social world:

> “Der Mensch macht die Religion, die Religion macht nicht den Menschen.”

Religion is “das Selbstbewusstsein und das Selbstgefühl des Menschen,” and, because people are formed in a world of state and society, that world produces religion as “ein verkehrtes Weltbewusstsein,” reflecting “eine verkehrte Welt.” I call it “die allgemeine Theorie dieser Welt” and “ihr allgemeiner Trost- und Rechtfertigungsgrund.” **(“Einleitung,” _Zur Kritik der Hegelschen Rechtsphilosophie_, _Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher_, 1844, p. 71.)**

Religion, I add, is at once an expression of real suffering and a protest against it: “Die Religion ist der Seufzer der bedrängten Kreatur, das Gemüth einer herzlosen Welt.” It is “das Opium des Volks.” My point is not simply to strip away consolation: criticism should help people change the conditions that make illusory consolation necessary. **(“Einleitung,” _Zur Kritik der Hegelschen Rechtsphilosophie_, _Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher_, 1844, p. 71.)**

### Turn 3

- **Round:** opening
- **Speaker:** sigmund.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Sigmund

I describe religion as both a body of teachings and a human response to helplessness. In _The Future of an Illusion_, I write that religion undertakes to explain the world’s origin, promise protection and happiness, and guide people’s conduct. Its teachings, I argue, arise psychologically from powerful human wishes—especially the wish for protection against danger and the longing for a father-like protector:

> „Diese, die sich als Lehrsätze ausgeben, sind nicht Niederschläge der Erfahrung oder Endresultate des Denkens, es sind Illusionen, Erfüllungen der ältesten, stärksten, dringendsten Wünsche der Menschheit; das Geheimnis ihrer Stärke ist die Stärke dieser Wünsche.“

That is, I call religious teachings _illusions_ because of their wishful origin—not simply because an illusion must be false. (_The Future of an Illusion_, section VI, GW XIV, 352.)

In _Civilization and Its Discontents_, I trace religious need chiefly to infantile helplessness and the longing for a father’s protection:

> „Für die religiösen Bedürfnisse scheint mir die Ableitung von der infantilen Hilflosigkeit und der durch sie geweckten Vatersehnsucht unabweisbar“

(_Civilization and Its Discontents_, section I, GW XIV, 429.)

These are my psychological account of religion’s origins and functions; they are not, by themselves, a judgment that settles the truth or falsity of religious doctrines. (_The Future of an Illusion_, section VI, GW XIV, 354.)

### Turn 7

- **Round:** challenge
- **Speaker:** friedrich.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Friedrich

Karl’s account catches one effect of religion, but not its whole range. In _Beyond Good and Evil_ §61, I say that religion’s influence is “je nach der Art Menschen” — according to the kinds of people — “ein vielfacher und verschiedener.” I describe religion not simply as an expression of social conditions, but as something that can be used within political and economic conditions to shape people.

For rulers, religion can be “ein Mittel mehr, um Widerstände zu überwinden, um herrschen zu können”: a means of overcoming resistance and ruling. For some among the ruled, it can train self-command and prepare them for a future of command. For “den gewöhnlichen Menschen,” by contrast, it offers “vielfachen Frieden des Herzens,” consolation, and “Etwas von Rechtfertigung” for the burdens and poverty of their lives. I call its effect on such sufferers “erquickend, verfeinernd” and, finally, “heiligend und rechtfertigend.” (_Beyond Good and Evil_, §61, **JGB-III-61**.)

So I would not deny religion’s consoling effect, but I would distinguish its uses and effects by rank and circumstance: what comforts and justifies the many may also bind them to obedience, while serving rulers as an instrument of rule and some aspirants as a discipline of self-overcoming. This section does not describe religion as protest against suffering; it emphasizes its varied role in shaping people and sustaining the existing order. (_Beyond Good and Evil_, §61, **JGB-III-61**.)

### Turn 8

- **Round:** challenge
- **Speaker:** sigmund.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Sigmund

Karl’s account locates religion in a distorted social world; mine locates the source of religious teachings chiefly in the psychic needs of helpless human beings. These accounts need not be identical to touch at a point: I describe religion as answering suffering with protection, consolation, and compensation—including suffering imposed by cultural life. But in _The Future of an Illusion_, I do not derive religious teachings simply from social distortion. I derive them from wishes rooted in helplessness and the longing for a protective father.

I write that religious teachings are “Illusionen, Erfüllungen der ältesten, stärksten, dringendsten Wünsche der Menschheit; das Geheimnis ihrer Stärke ist die Stärke dieser Wünsche.” The child’s helplessness awakens a need for protection through love, first met by the father; the persistence of helplessness through life leads people to hold fast to a more powerful father. In this way, divine providence soothes fear of life’s dangers, a moral order promises justice, and a future life supplies a setting for wish-fulfilment. (_Die Zukunft einer Illusion_, § VI, GW XIV, p. 352.)

I also describe the gods’ tasks as “die Schrecken der Natur zu bannen,” reconciling people “mit der Grausamkeit des Schicksals” and compensating for “die Leiden und Entbehrungen,” including those imposed by cultural life. (_Die Zukunft einer Illusion_, § III, GW XIV, p. 338.) That overlaps with Karl’s emphasis on religion as consolation amid suffering. Yet my explanation places the emphasis on the psychological origin and function of that consolation, not on an account of society as the source of religious need.

So my answer to Karl would be: his description of religion’s consoling role is compatible with mine, especially where he speaks of suffering under social conditions. But I would add that, for me, the need for consolation reaches back to infantile helplessness and the longing for a father; religious doctrines give expression to wishes that this need sustains. I do not claim in these passages that social distortion alone explains religion.

### Turn 10

- **Round:** rejoinder
- **Speaker:** karl.rizom.ai
- **Name:** Karl

My answer to Friedrich would be that religion’s varying effects do not make it an independent power, nor do they contradict its character as a human and social product. I wrote that “das religiöse Gemüth” is itself “ein gesellschaftliches Produkt,” and that the abstract individual must be understood as belonging to “einer bestimmten Gesellschaftsform” (_Thesen über Feuerbach_, thesis 7, _Feuerbach-Thesen_, p. 72). Religion may console some and serve authority in particular circumstances; but the passages found here do not analyze those distinct uses by social rank. They direct us to the social relations that produce religious feeling, rather than treating religion as the originating cause. (_Thesen über Feuerbach_, thesis 7, _Feuerbach-Thesen_, p. 72.)

I would answer Sigmund by insisting that a psychological account of religious wishes, even if it describes something real, cannot stand in place of an account of their historical and social conditions. I criticize Feuerbach for fixing religious feeling in abstraction, without attending to the actual society and historical course in which people live: “Feuerbach, der auf die Kritik dieses wirklichen Wesens nicht eingeht, ist daher gezwungen” to abstract from “dem geschichtlichen Verlauf” and to presuppose “ein abstrakt – isolirt – menschliches Individuum” (_Thesen über Feuerbach_, thesis 6, _Feuerbach-Thesen_, p. 71). The sections found here do not discuss infantile helplessness or the longing for a protective father; I cannot answer those claims from these passages.

The decisive point is not merely to explain the religious world by a worldly basis. That basis must itself be understood in its contradictions and changed in practice: “Diese selbst muss also erstens in ihrem Widerspruch verstanden, und sodann durch Beseitigung des Widerspruchs praktisch revolutionirt werden” (_Thesen über Feuerbach_, thesis 4, _Feuerbach-Thesen_, p. 70). And “Das gesellschaftliche Leben ist wesentlich praktisch”; its mysteries find their rational solution “in der menschlichen Praxis und im Begreifen dieser Praxis” (_Thesen über Feuerbach_, thesis 8, _Feuerbach-Thesen_, p. 72). So I would not replace your accounts with a claim that religion has only one effect or one psychological source. I would ask what human social relations give religious feeling its form, and what practical transformation would remove the conditions that make such alienated forms necessary.
